rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God accepted Job’s prayer about his physical distress, restored his health, gave him children, and restored his former grandeur.
rows.anchor: The Almighty accepted the supplication of Job (sws) mentioned in the words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Job asked only about his bodily affliction, regarding restored health as enough; God’s grace gave him more than he thought himself worthy to receive.
rows.anchor: he regarded his desire to be more than met

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God reunited Job with family members dispersed during the trial, replaced those who had died, and increased his followers.
rows.anchor: God gathered his family members who had dispersed in this period of trial

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The restoration is presented as God’s unexpected favour and as a lasting reminder of His favours to worshippers who remain attached to Him in hardship and ease.
rows.anchor: whatever happened, happened because of God’s favour

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shared traits of Ishmael and Idris were discussed earlier in Maryam, verses 54–57.
rows.anchor: The similarity of traits these two prophets have has been alluded to there.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text calls all three prophets steadfast, indicating that patience was a special quality they shared.
rows.anchor: about all the three is it stated that they were very patient.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ishmael’s patience is well known, and the Qur’an alludes to it in several places.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ ān has alluded to it at several instances.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author knows no reliable life history for Idris or Dhul-Kifl and notes their names are absent from ancient scriptures; perhaps their names changed in Arabic or were erased and restored by the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: These names are not mentioned in ancient scriptures.

rows.speaker: Some people
rows.claim: Some identify Dhul-Kifl with Ezekiel, but the author says this can be accepted only if Ezekiel is known to have borne that title.
rows.anchor: Some people think that Dhū al-Kifl is actually Ezekiel (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Neither the Qur’an nor the Torah records every prophet or their life story; God alone knows all of them.
rows.anchor: neither the Qur’ ān nor the Torah mentions all the prophets and their life histories.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhu al-Nun means “companion of the fish”: Jonah received the title after being swallowed, and it also conveys affection.
rows.anchor: which means “companion of the fish.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah was sent to Nineveh; its population of 120,000 in the Book of Jonah accords with Qur’an 37:147, which says 100,000 or more.
rows.anchor: This corroborates the Biblical account.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After long preaching met rejection, Jonah left in dejection, thinking there was no point in enduring hardship among people who ignored him; such despair is natural for a truthful person.
rows.anchor: he left them. He thought that when he could not penetrate into these stone-hearted people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A messenger may leave his people only by God’s decision and permission; God knows when a nation can no longer accept truth and when it should face punishment.
rows.anchor: messenger cannot leave his nation without God’s permission

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah thought he had discharged his duty after warning his people and could consign them to God and migrate, expecting relief from his trial.
rows.anchor: he had fulfilled his obligation before God and he should consign such a wretched nation to Him and migrate from them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah’s thought came from pure zeal for truth, but the trial God had set for his people still had to run its course.
rows.anchor: the trials which the Almighty has subjected his people to are bound to take their course.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disenchanted with his people, Jonah boarded a departing ship, which later encountered a storm.
rows.anchor: he embarked on a ship which was about to set off for a journey. After sailing for sometime, the ship was caught in a storm.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sailors followed a superstition that a runaway slave aboard caused the storm and that throwing him overboard would end it.
rows.anchor: he was thrown overboard, they would not be delivered from the storm.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lots were cast, and the author says Jonah was assigned to cast them, perhaps because the sailors considered him most respectable; the lot fell on Jonah and he was thrown overboard.
rows.anchor: it was Jonah (sws) who was given the responsibility of casting lots.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A large fish, probably a whale, swallowed Jonah; when he saw his escape attempt had brought him into greater darkness, he prayed sincerely from the heart.
rows.anchor: A large fish, most probably a whale, swallowed him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God accepted Jonah’s sincere prayer, the fish cast him ashore, and God grew a pumpkin-like plant to shade his weakened body.
rows.anchor: the fish cast him on the sandy shore. There, in order to save his emaciated body from the heat of the sun

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Jonah recovered, God sent him again to warn Nineveh; the withered sheltering plant made him grieve, and God taught him to consider the people He had created and raised.
rows.anchor: if he has been aggrieved by the withering away of a trivial creeper

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God directed Jonah back to Nineveh, where his renewed warning moved everyone from ordinary people to the king to profess faith and repent.
rows.anchor: Such was the profound effect of his call that everyone from the common man to the king started to tremble.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king removed his royal robe, put on sackcloth, and ordered the people to abandon evil, fast, plead to God, and repent.
rows.anchor: The king took off his royal robe and attired himself in sackcloth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reconstructs Jonah’s account to correct exegetes’ confused reports, relying on indications and statements in the Bible and Qur’an and pointing readers to al-Saffat for more.
rows.anchor: I have presented the above details to give its true picture.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object of “angry” is suppressed because context makes clear that Jonah left his nation while sad and angry.
rows.anchor: because of concomitant indications. The implication is: he left his nation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah left in anger because he had done all he could to warn his people, but they ignored him, humiliated truth, and mocked his message.
rows.anchor: he did all that he could to warn them, but they completely ignored him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah thought that leaving could deliver him from the affliction his nation had put him through.
rows.anchor: he thought that in this manner he would be able to deliver himself from the trial his nation had put him through.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah’s zeal made him overlook that God had commissioned him; deserting without God’s permission could expose him to a greater trial.
rows.anchor: if he deserts it without His permission, he could face an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah did not think he could escape God’s accountability; he hoped to distance himself from wicked people and live peacefully, but a messenger is like a soldier who cannot leave his post without permission.
rows.anchor: This thought in itself is not a sin, but a messenger, as just indicated, is like a soldier deputed at a front.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the act seemed innocent, it implied that Jonah could escape God’s trial by his own choice; God exposed this hidden implication to correct him.
rows.anchor: This hidden aspect was not evident to Jonah (sws). For this reason, it was made plain before him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person can miss the mistaken idea implicit in an innocent act until a wise guide points it out; God corrects messengers because they exemplify conduct for humanity and even slight deviations can have far-reaching consequences.
rows.anchor: Since messengers of God are an example for all mankind, even a slight deviation from them is checked by God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers this reading as reasonable and free of blame toward Jonah; it avoids the exegetes’ strained linguistic reinterpretations, which still failed to solve the difficulty.
rows.anchor: This interpretation is in consonance with the norms sense and reason and also does not entail any blame on Jonah (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ship’s details are omitted and only Jonah’s prayer in the fish’s belly is reported so the account can stress God’s acceptance of a servant’s plea in hopeless danger, provided he trusts and calls only on God.
rows.anchor: the purpose is not to divulge its details but to show that the gracious God accepts the supplications of His servant

rows.speaker: Book of Jonah
rows.claim: The Bible’s Book of Jonah gives a parallel prayer in which Jonah calls to the Lord from distress and says his cry was heard.
rows.anchor: In the Book of Jonah of the Bible, this supplication is mentioned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural “darknesses” intensifies and expands the darkness; Arabic plurals can express vastness, as in al-Mashariq and al-Magharib, and here denotes darkness in the fish’s belly and deep sea.
rows.anchor: in the Arabic language, at times a plural denotes vastness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording shows that God does not need a public forum or broadcast technology to hear a servant’s call in the deep sea.
rows.anchor: The purpose is to show that no one should be misled by the fact that God needs a public forum

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God hears and answers His servants’ cries even in the pitch darkness of the deep sea.
rows.anchor: He listens to the cries of His servants in the pitch darkness of the deep sea and responds to them.

words: أَن لَّآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّآ أَنتَ سُبْحَٰنَكَ إِنِّى كُنتُ مِنَ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah asked for nothing in the prayer; he confessed his fault and entrusted the matter to his Lord, whose verdict would be best, wise, and merciful.
rows.anchor: Jonah (sws) has not expressed any desire or demand; he only expressed and confessed his mistake.

words: أَن لَّآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّآ أَنتَ سُبْحَٰنَكَ إِنِّى كُنتُ مِنَ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer first affirms that only God deserves worship and obedience and that all matters return to Him, then declares Him free of defect and admits Jonah wronged himself rather than God wronging him.
rows.anchor: First of all, he expressed that only God is worthy of worship and obedience and all matters turn to Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Jonah did not state a request, God, who knows the unseen and hears even ocean-depth prayers, relieved his distress; that distress included both the ship and the circumstances that led him to leave his people.
rows.anchor: all his stress and sorrow was relieved by the God Who knows the unseen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elsewhere the Qur’an says that when Jonah preached again, his people believed and the threatened punishment was averted.
rows.anchor: when he preached his nation a second time, all of them embraced faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise to deliver believers addresses Muhammad and his companions in their revelation-era hardship: they should not despair, since God hears sincere pleas, lifts grief, brings dark days to an end, and will make truth prevail and their people believe.
rows.anchor: these incidents have not been narrated without a purpose. They are meant to assure Prophet Muḥammad (sws) and his companions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zachariah’s story is detailed in Maryam: he also prayed in apparently hopeless circumstances, and God made the impossible possible despite his infertile wife.
rows.anchor: He too supplicated before God in apparently very hopeless circumstances.
